newsitem.title: USA: Trans-World slams Russian aluminum takeover call.
newsitem.headline: Trans-World slams Russian aluminum takeover call.

text.p: A call by the Russia's Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov to curb foreign ownership in the aluminum industry was contrary to the Gore-Chernomyrdin Commission on opening the country's economy to international trade and investment, privately-held Trans-World Group said.

"If this Russian takeover agenda is allowed to succeed, it will close the book on what would have been substantial progress and a real East-West partnership envisioned during the past four years by the Gore-Chernomyrdin Commission," Trans-World chairman, David Reuben said in a full page letter published in Sunday's edition of the New York Times.
The letter was addressed to U.S. Vice president Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister, Viktor Chernomyrdin.

On February 21 Reuters reported Kulikov's address to the Russian State Duma lower parliament house. He said Russia should consider slapping duties on imports of raw materials used in primary aluminum production.

In a copy of the address obtained by Reuters at the time, Kulikov also said Russia should look at tightening federal bodies' control over tolling deals which involve importing alumina, the intermedite product used to make aluminum.
Trans-World is a leading importer of alumina into Russia and owns a substantial stake in Russian aluminum production.
Reuben described himself as one of the largest foreign investors and employers in Russia, and one of the first to enter the country six years ago.
"We made long term investments of hundreds of millions of dollars in plant, equipment and operations to revitalize Russia's moribund aluminum and steel industries," Reuben wrote.
The company did not seek majority control in any company.
"The record will show that with our Russian national team, we turned these industries profitably around into well-run, productive enterprises," Reuben added.
Russia was suffering from a "craven, political power play", aimed at confiscating certain foreign investments and facilities without due process, Reuben said.

The power play was led by officials within the Ministry of Interior and by renegade Russian banks, Reuben charged. Such moves in the aluminum industry would jeapordize all private foreign investment in Russia.

While short on detail, Kulikov's comments reflected concern within the domestic aluminum industry that it is losing out on hard currency earnings by producing much of its aluminum under tolling deals.
However, some Russian smelters are dogged by cash shortages and cannot afford to buy the alumina themselves to process into metal for sale.
